questions.title: Always Encrypted vs. Always Encrypted with Secure Enclaves
questions.prompt: A healthcare client needs to encrypt SSNs and diagnosis codes so that even DBAs with sysadmin can't see plaintext, but they also need to run range queries and pattern matches against those columns for case management reports. Explain why standard Always Encrypted can't satisfy both requirements, and what Secure Enclaves actually change.
questions.modelAnswer: Standard Always Encrypted comes in two column encryption types, deterministic and randomized, and the client's two requirements each rule out one of them. Deterministic encryption produces the same ciphertext for the same plaintext value every time, which allows equality comparisons and joins to happen server-side without the server ever seeing plaintext — but it leaks a pattern (identical ciphertexts for identical values), and critically it does not support range comparisons (>, <, BETWEEN) or LIKE pattern matching, because the server has no way to compare ciphertext ordering or substrings without decrypting first. Randomized encryption is more secure (no repeatable pattern) but doesn't even support equality comparisons server-side, let alone ranges. So with standard Always Encrypted, any range query or LIKE match on an encrypted column has to pull all rows back to the client and filter in application memory after decryption, which is often not viable for a reporting workload. Secure Enclaves change this by introducing a hardware- or software-isolated enclave inside the SQL Server/Azure SQL process itself — a memory region that even the database engine's own privileged processes can't inspect — where encrypted data can be decrypted temporarily, computed on (comparisons, pattern matches, even in-place encryption for initial column setup), and the result re-encrypted, all without the plaintext ever being observable outside the enclave, including by a sysadmin running a debugger against the SQL Server process. That's what actually satisfies both requirements at once: the DBA genuinely cannot see plaintext at any point, yet range queries and LIKE predicates can be pushed into the enclave and executed server-side. The tradeoff is operational: enclaves require specific compute tiers/configuration, attestation setup (for VBS enclaves) adds deployment complexity, and enclave-enabled computations carry a performance cost versus a predicate that could run directly against deterministic ciphertext.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain it as: standard Always Encrypted gives you a choice, not a solution to both problems at once. Deterministic lets the server do equality joins without seeing plaintext, but it can't do ranges or LIKE — the server literally cannot compare ciphertext order or substrings. Randomized is safer but can't even do equality server-side. So for range queries on an encrypted SSN column, standard Always Encrypted means pulling everything back and filtering client-side, which isn't realistic for a reporting workload. Secure Enclaves are the actual answer here — they carve out a region inside the SQL Server process that's isolated even from a sysadmin, decrypt inside that enclave just long enough to run the comparison, and hand back a result without plaintext ever being visible outside it. I'd be upfront with the client that this isn't free — there's attestation and compute-tier requirements to set up, and enclave computations cost more than a plain deterministic equality check — but it's the only standard SQL Server feature that gets them 'DBA can't see it' and 'can still run range queries' at the same time.
commonMistakes: Assumes standard Always Encrypted supports range queries if you just pick the 'right' encryption type
Confuses deterministic encryption's equality support with range/LIKE support
Describes Secure Enclaves as 'just better encryption' without explaining the isolated-computation mechanism
Omits the operational cost (attestation, compute tier requirements, performance) of enclaves
keyPoints: Explains deterministic vs randomized Always Encrypted and their query limitations
Correctly states neither standard mode supports server-side range/LIKE queries
Explains the enclave as an isolated compute region even sysadmin can't observe
Notes enclave-enabled columns can support richer in-place computation (range, pattern matching, initial encryption)
Flags the real deployment/performance tradeoffs of enclaves

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Always Encrypted's deterministic/randomized limitations
Correctly explains what Secure Enclaves add and why it solves the stated problem
Identifies realistic operational tradeoffs of enclaves
Answer is specific to the healthcare range-query/LIKE scenario, not generic

questions.title: Transparent Data Encryption: Service-Managed vs. Customer-Managed Keys
questions.prompt: A financial services client's compliance team insists on 'full control over encryption keys' for Transparent Data Encryption, including the ability to revoke access and prove key rotation. Explain the difference between service-managed and customer-managed (BYOK) TDE keys, and what operational responsibility the client is actually taking on by choosing BYOK.
questions.modelAnswer: TDE encrypts data at rest at the page level using a database encryption key (DEK), which is itself protected by a server-level certificate or asymmetric key — this outer protector is what differs between the two models. With service-managed TDE, Azure generates and manages that protector automatically; Microsoft handles its storage, rotation, and backup entirely behind the scenes, and the client has no visibility into or control over it. With customer-managed keys (BYOK), the client generates or imports an asymmetric key into Azure Key Vault, and Azure SQL is configured to use that Key Vault key as the TDE protector instead of the service-managed one. This satisfies 'full control' in a real, auditable sense: the client's security team controls the key's lifecycle (creation, rotation schedule, expiration), can view every access to it through Key Vault's diagnostic logging, and — critically — can revoke the key's permissions or disable it entirely, which immediately makes the database's data inaccessible, functioning as a genuine kill switch. But that control comes with real operational responsibility the client needs to understand: if the Key Vault key is deleted or access is revoked without an intentional, coordinated plan, the database goes offline, because TDE can't decrypt pages without it — this is a self-inflicted outage risk, not just a theoretical one. The client also now owns key rotation: Azure doesn't silently rotate a customer-managed key, so a rotation policy has to be designed and tested, and the Key Vault itself needs its own availability design (soft-delete and purge protection enabled, so an accidental deletion doesn't become permanent and unrecoverable), plus an access policy that doesn't let the same compromised identity both access the database and administer the key. I'd walk the compliance team through this explicitly: BYOK gives them the control and auditability they're asking for, but it moves key-lifecycle operations onto their team, and a mistake there has a much sharper consequence than a service-managed key ever could.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd tell the compliance team: yes, BYOK gets you what you're asking for, but I want you to understand what you're signing up to operate, not just what you're gaining. With service-managed keys, Microsoft handles the whole lifecycle and you have zero visibility — fine for most workloads, but it's genuinely not 'full control.' With customer-managed keys in Key Vault, you get the real thing: you can see every access in the logs, you control rotation, and you can revoke it as an actual kill switch. The part I always spell out before anyone signs off is that the kill switch cuts both ways — if someone fat-fingers a key deletion or a permission change without a plan, the database goes offline immediately, because TDE literally can't read the data without that key. So I'd insist on soft-delete and purge protection on the Key Vault from day one, a tested rotation runbook, and access policies that don't let one compromised identity touch both the database and the key that protects it. BYOK is the right call for a compliance requirement like this — I just don't want the team finding out about the operational side the hard way.
commonMistakes: Describes BYOK as 'more secure' without explaining the operational responsibility shift
Doesn't mention the outage risk if the customer-managed key is revoked or deleted without planning
Omits Key Vault soft-delete/purge protection as a prerequisite for safely using BYOK
Fails to explain that rotation is now the client's responsibility, not automatic
keyPoints: Explains TDE's DEK and the server-level protector (certificate/key) it depends on
Correctly distinguishes service-managed vs. customer-managed (Key Vault) protectors
Explains the real auditability/revocation benefit of BYOK
Flags the outage risk and operational ownership (rotation, soft-delete/purge protection) that come with BYOK

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains TDE's key hierarchy and the protector's role
Correctly distinguishes service-managed vs. customer-managed keys
Identifies the genuine compliance benefit (revocation, auditability)
Honestly addresses the operational risk/responsibility BYOK introduces

questions.title: Dynamic Data Masking, Row-Level Security, or Always Encrypted — Picking the Right Control
questions.prompt: A customer support application needs: (1) support agents to see customer records but not full credit card numbers, (2) regional sales reps to only ever see rows for their own region even if they write ad-hoc queries, and (3) a column that even the DBA team should never see in plaintext. Map each requirement to the correct Azure SQL security feature and explain why the other two wouldn't work for that requirement.
questions.modelAnswer: These are three genuinely different threat models, and each maps to exactly one feature because the others don't address that specific threat. Requirement 1 — agents seeing a masked credit card — is Dynamic Data Masking (DDM): it obscures the display of a column's value for users without the UNMASK permission while leaving the underlying data fully queryable and unencrypted in storage, which is exactly what's needed for a support UI that needs to show 'ending in 1234' without exposing the full number. DDM would fail requirement 2 because it masks a column's value, not which rows are visible — a rep could still see every region's rows, just with some column obscured, which doesn't satisfy 'only their own region.' It also fails requirement 3, because DDM is purely a display-layer control — anyone with elevated permission (including a DBA with the right grant, or anyone querying with sufficient rights, or even a moderately careless use of a bypassing tool) can see the real value; it was never designed to stop a privileged DBA. Requirement 2 — reps restricted to their own region's rows regardless of how they query — is Row-Level Security (RLS): a security policy with a predicate function evaluated on every query against the table, filtering or blocking rows based on session context like a region claim, enforced at the engine level so it applies even to ad-hoc SELECT * queries, not just application-layer filters. RLS doesn't help requirement 1, because it filters rows, not columns — a rep within their allowed region would still see the full credit card number if nothing else protects that column. It doesn't help requirement 3 either, because RLS doesn't touch column content at all; a sysadmin or a user with db_owner can always see the predicate-filtered rows' actual column values, and RLS predicates are often also bypassable by sysadmin via session context manipulation unless carefully designed. Requirement 3 — a column even the DBA team must never see in plaintext — is Always Encrypted: the encryption and decryption happen entirely in the client driver, so plaintext never exists inside SQL Server's process at all, not even in memory, meaning sysadmin, DBA, and anyone with full database permissions genuinely cannot see it, which is the one property DDM and RLS don't provide. Always Encrypted would be overkill and operationally wrong for requirement 1 (it would block the support UI from doing any partial display formatting without specific coding) and does nothing for requirement 2 at all, since it protects column content, not row visibility.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd walk through each one by asking 'what's actually being protected from whom.' For the agents and the masked card number, that's a display problem — the data's fine to exist in the clear in the database, we just don't want it shown by default, so that's Dynamic Data Masking. It wouldn't help with the regional restriction, because masking a column does nothing about which rows show up, and it's not meant to stop a privileged user at all, which rules it out for the DBA-can't-see-it requirement too. For the regional reps, the threat is 'someone writes their own query and sees rows they shouldn't,' which is a row-visibility problem the application layer can't reliably enforce on its own — that's Row-Level Security, because it's a predicate evaluated by the engine on every query, ad-hoc or not. It wouldn't touch the card-number masking problem since it's about rows, not columns, and a DBA with sufficient rights can still see everything RLS lets through. And for the column the DBA team genuinely can't see — that's the one case where masking and RLS both fail, because neither stops someone with the right permission from seeing real data. Always Encrypted is the only one where the plaintext never exists inside the engine's process, full stop, which is the actual guarantee that requirement needs.
commonMistakes: Suggests DDM can restrict row visibility, confusing column masking with row filtering
Assumes RLS protects against privileged users (sysadmin/db_owner) seeing data, when it does not reliably by default
Recommends Always Encrypted for the masking or row-filtering requirement, over-engineering a display or row-visibility problem
Doesn't explain why the DBA-can't-see-it requirement specifically rules out DDM and RLS
keyPoints: Correctly maps masking (agents/display) -> DDM, row filtering (region) -> RLS, true plaintext protection -> Always Encrypted
Explains why DDM doesn't stop privileged users and doesn't filter rows
Explains why RLS filters rows but doesn't protect column content from privileged users
Explains why Always Encrypted is the only one that removes plaintext from the engine's process entirely

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly maps all three requirements to the right feature
Correctly explains why DDM fails the other two requirements
Correctly explains why RLS fails the other two requirements
Correctly explains why Always Encrypted is uniquely suited to requirement 3

questions.title: DTU vs. vCore at Enterprise Scale: Governance, Cost, and Predictability
questions.prompt: A platform team managing 200+ Azure SQL databases across business units is deciding whether to standardize on the DTU or vCore purchasing model going forward. Explain the real differences beyond the pricing page, and what you'd actually recommend for an organization at this scale.
questions.modelAnswer: DTU bundles compute, memory, and I/O into a single abstracted unit per tier (Basic/Standard/Premium), which makes initial sizing simple but gives the platform team almost no independent control over which resource is actually the bottleneck for a given workload — a database that's memory-starved but CPU-light still has to move up an entire DTU tier, paying for CPU and I/O it doesn't need, to get the memory it does. vCore lets compute (vCores, generation) and storage be sized and scaled independently, and it maps far more directly onto what a DBA actually diagnoses with DMVs — 'this database needs more memory for its buffer pool' is an answerable, actionable statement in vCore terms, and a vague one in DTU terms. At 200+ databases across business units, three things matter beyond raw pricing: first, vCore is the only model that supports Azure Hybrid Benefit, letting the organization apply existing SQL Server licenses for a substantial discount — at this scale that's often the single largest cost lever available, and it's simply unavailable under DTU; second, vCore-based elastic pools and reserved capacity give the platform team real levers for cost governance and chargeback across business units, because compute and storage can be tracked, forecast, and rightsized per workload rather than per bundled tier; third, vCore surfaces Hyperscale and serverless options that DTU doesn't, which matters as some of those 200 databases inevitably grow past what a Premium DTU tier can handle gracefully. My actual recommendation would be to standardize new provisioning on vCore going forward — not because DTU is 'wrong', but because an organization managing a large, heterogeneous fleet needs the independent compute/storage scaling, licensing flexibility, and tiering options vCore provides, and mixing both models indefinitely creates two different mental models and two different cost-governance processes for the platform team to maintain. For the existing DTU databases, I'd migrate opportunistically during their next sizing review rather than as a disruptive mass migration, since the DTU-to-vCore conversion is online and low-risk per database.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd steer them away from thinking about this as a pricing comparison and toward thinking about it as a governance decision. DTU is simple because it's one dial, but at 200+ databases across different business units, one dial means the platform team can't tell a team 'you specifically need more memory, not more CPU' — they just have to move up a whole tier and absorb the cost of resources they don't need. vCore splits that apart, and it also happens to be the only path to Hybrid Benefit, which at this scale is usually real money on the table if the org already owns SQL Server licenses. I'd recommend standardizing new databases on vCore, partly for that licensing lever and partly because it gives the platform team an actual cost-governance story per business unit instead of a bundled tier they can't decompose. I wouldn't go rip out all the existing DTU databases on day one, though — that's a disruptive migration for marginal near-term benefit. I'd fold the conversion into each database's next normal sizing review, since it's a low-risk, mostly online change per database.
commonMistakes: Compares DTU and vCore purely on sticker price without mentioning Hybrid Benefit
Doesn't explain that DTU bundles resources while vCore allows independent compute/storage sizing
Recommends a disruptive mass migration off DTU instead of an opportunistic, low-risk approach
Fails to connect the choice to organization-scale concerns like chargeback and cost governance
keyPoints: Explains DTU as a bundled resource abstraction vs. vCore's independent compute/storage model
Identifies Azure Hybrid Benefit as a vCore-only lever, often decisive at scale
Connects the choice to cost governance/chargeback across business units
Recommends a practical, low-disruption migration path for existing DTU databases

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the structural difference between DTU and vCore
Identifies Hybrid Benefit and licensing as a key enterprise-scale factor
Gives a clear, justified recommendation for the organization
Proposes a sensible, low-risk migration approach for existing databases

questions.title: When Hyperscale Is (and Isn't) the Right Service Tier
questions.prompt: A client has a 6 TB transactional database on General Purpose that's starting to see slow backups and occasional storage-related throttling, and someone on their team has already decided 'we need Hyperscale.' Explain how Hyperscale's architecture actually solves (or doesn't solve) their stated problems, and what you'd verify before agreeing with that recommendation.
questions.modelAnswer: Hyperscale's architecture separates compute from storage far more aggressively than General Purpose or Business Critical: data is split across a scalable layer of page servers, each independently caching and serving a shard of the database, with the log service streaming transaction log records to those page servers and to long-term storage asynchronously, rather than a single compute node owning and backing up the entire data file. Two specific claims in the client's problem map directly onto this architecture, and one needs verification rather than assumption. Slow, full-copy backups are solved structurally: Hyperscale backups are near-instantaneous file snapshots at the storage layer regardless of database size, because there's no multi-hour full copy operation the way there is on General Purpose at 6 TB — this genuinely addresses their stated backup problem. Storage-related throttling is more nuanced: on General Purpose, storage throughput is tied to the provisioned compute tier, so growth past certain data sizes can hit IOPS/throughput ceilings tied to compute size, not raw storage capacity, and Hyperscale's page-server architecture removes that specific coupling by scaling storage throughput with the number of page servers rather than the compute tier — so if their throttling is genuinely storage-throughput-related, Hyperscale addresses it; but if what they're calling 'throttling' is actually log-write throughput or DTU/vCore compute saturation during peak load, Hyperscale doesn't inherently fix that, since compute sizing still matters for CPU/memory-bound workloads. Before agreeing with the recommendation, I'd verify three things: pull the actual resource/storage metrics (via Azure Monitor and sys.dm_db_resource_stats) to confirm whether the throttling is storage I/O, log write throughput, or compute, since only the right diagnosis tells you whether Hyperscale actually fixes it or just changes the backup story while leaving the real bottleneck untouched; check whether the workload relies on features Hyperscale doesn't fully support at the time of evaluation (certain cross-database transactions, some replication scenarios); and confirm the team understands Hyperscale's named replica model for read scale-out and HA, since migrating tiers is also a good moment to redesign for that capability rather than just lifting-and-shifting the same architecture onto new storage.
questions.professionalAnswer: I wouldn't just agree because 6 TB sounds like a Hyperscale-shaped number. I'd say: let's confirm what's actually throttling first, because Hyperscale fixes a very specific set of problems, and I want to know we're hitting one of them before we commit to a migration. The backup story is genuinely solved by Hyperscale's architecture — backups become near-instant snapshots instead of a multi-hour full copy, full stop, that's real and I'd tell them so. The throttling claim needs more digging — if it's storage IOPS or throughput tied to their current compute tier, Hyperscale's page-server design does remove that ceiling. But if what they're actually hitting is compute or log-write saturation during peak load, moving to Hyperscale doesn't make that go away, because compute sizing still matters there. So before I sign off, I'm pulling the actual resource stats to see which bottleneck we're really looking at, and I'm also using the migration conversation as a chance to ask whether they should be designing in named replicas for read scale-out, since that's a real capability Hyperscale adds that's worth architecting for on purpose, not just inheriting by accident.
commonMistakes: Agrees with 'we need Hyperscale' based on database size alone without diagnosing the actual bottleneck
Assumes Hyperscale fixes all forms of throttling, including compute/CPU-bound bottlenecks it doesn't address
Doesn't mention Hyperscale's backup advantage as a near-instant snapshot versus a full copy
Misses the opportunity to discuss named replicas as part of the migration decision
keyPoints: Explains Hyperscale's page-server/log-service architecture at a mechanism level
Correctly attributes the backup improvement to storage-layer snapshotting
Distinguishes storage-throughput throttling (which Hyperscale addresses) from compute-bound bottlenecks (which it doesn't)
Proposes verifying the actual bottleneck via resource metrics before committing to the migration
Mentions named replicas as a related architectural consideration

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Hyperscale's architecture and how it changes backups
Correctly distinguishes which throttling scenarios Hyperscale does/doesn't solve
Proposes concrete verification steps before committing to the recommendation
Shows awareness of broader Hyperscale capabilities (named replicas)

questions.title: Resource Governor for Workload Isolation on a Shared Managed Instance
questions.prompt: A single Azure SQL Managed Instance hosts both a high-priority OLTP application and a lower-priority internal reporting workload, and the reporting queries occasionally starve the OLTP app of CPU and memory during month-end. Explain how Resource Governor would address this, and what it would not solve.
questions.modelAnswer: Resource Governor lets you define resource pools, each with configurable CPU, memory, and I/O limits (minimum guarantees and maximum caps), and workload groups that classify incoming sessions into those pools based on a classifier function evaluated at logon — typically on login name, application name, or host name. For this scenario, the fix is to create a lower-priority resource pool capped at a modest CPU/memory ceiling for the reporting workload's login or application name, and either a dedicated higher-priority pool with a guaranteed minimum for the OLTP application, or simply leave OLTP on the default pool while capping reporting, so reporting can never consume more than its ceiling even under contention, protecting the OLTP app's headroom during month-end. This genuinely solves resource contention between workloads sharing the same instance — it's the correct, supported mechanism for that specific problem, and it requires no application changes, only a classifier function and pool/group configuration. What Resource Governor does not solve: it doesn't fix a reporting query that's slow because of a missing index or a bad execution plan — it just limits how much of the instance that slow query can consume while it runs, so the report will still be slow, just less disruptive to everyone else; it doesn't eliminate lock contention or blocking between the two workloads if they're touching the same tables, since locking is independent of CPU/memory pool limits; and it doesn't replace proper workload separation (a read replica or separate instance) if the reporting workload's resource needs grow to the point where even a capped pool still meaningfully competes for the instance's total capacity — Resource Governor manages contention within a shared instance's existing capacity, it doesn't create more capacity. I'd present it as the right first move for this specific symptom, paired with a note that if reporting keeps growing, the long-term answer is workload separation, not progressively tighter pools.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd explain Resource Governor as putting guardrails on a shared instance, not as a performance fix for either workload individually. The mechanism is: a classifier function looks at who's logging in — login name, app name, whatever's reliable — and routes them into a resource pool with a CPU and memory ceiling. So for this case, I'd cap the reporting workload's pool low enough that it can't eat into what OLTP needs during month-end, and that directly solves the resource-contention symptom they're describing, with zero app changes. What I'd be careful to say clearly is what it doesn't fix — if the reporting query is slow because of a missing index, Resource Governor doesn't make it fast, it just makes sure its slowness stays contained instead of dragging OLTP down with it. It also doesn't touch blocking if the two workloads happen to be locking the same rows — that's a separate problem. And I'd flag that this is a contention fix within the instance's existing capacity, not a capacity increase — if reporting keeps growing, at some point the real answer is a separate instance or a read replica, not an ever-tighter pool.
commonMistakes: Describes Resource Governor as fixing query performance rather than managing resource contention between workloads
Doesn't mention the classifier function as the mechanism that routes sessions into pools
Assumes Resource Governor also resolves blocking/locking contention, which it does not
Treats pool capping as a permanent substitute for workload separation instead of a near-term mitigation
keyPoints: Explains resource pools, workload groups, and the classifier function mechanism
Correctly proposes capping the reporting pool to protect OLTP headroom
Clarifies that Resource Governor doesn't fix slow queries or blocking, only resource contention
Notes the long-term limit: it manages contention within existing capacity, doesn't add capacity

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Resource Governor's mechanism (pools, groups, classifier)
Correctly applies it to solve the stated contention problem
Accurately identifies what it does NOT solve (query performance, blocking)
Frames it as near-term mitigation vs. long-term workload separation

questions.title: Hunting Query Regressions Across a Fleet With Query Store, Not One Database at a Time
questions.prompt: You support 40 Azure SQL databases for one client. Rather than waiting for a complaint about a specific database, describe how you'd use Query Store proactively to find performance regressions across the whole fleet, and what you'd automate so this doesn't depend on someone remembering to look.
questions.modelAnswer: Query Store, once enabled per database (it's on by default for Azure SQL Database), persists the history of query execution plans and their runtime statistics — duration, CPU, logical reads, memory grant — bucketed over time intervals, which is exactly the data needed to detect 'this query used to run in X ms and now runs in Y ms' without having to catch it live via a DMV snapshot. At fleet scale, the proactive approach is to query sys.query_store_runtime_stats and sys.query_store_plan (joined to sys.query_store_query/query_text) on a schedule against every database, comparing a recent window's average/P95 duration for each query_id against an earlier baseline window, and surfacing any query where that ratio crosses a meaningful threshold — I'd set the threshold relative (e.g., 2x regression) rather than absolute, since a 50ms-to-150ms regression on a rarely-run report matters far less than the same ratio on something called thousands of times an hour, so I'd also weight by execution count. Rather than running this manually against 40 databases, I'd automate it as a PowerShell script (using dbatools' Invoke-DbaQuery or straight Az SQL cmdlets to enumerate every database on every logical server under the client's subscription) that runs this comparison query against each database, aggregates the results into a single report, and only pages or emails the team when a regression crosses the threshold — turning this into an exception-based alert rather than something anyone has to remember to check. I'd schedule that script via Azure Automation (a runbook on a timer trigger) rather than relying on a local scheduled task, so it runs reliably regardless of anyone's laptop, and I'd log every run's output to a central table or Log Analytics workspace so regression history itself becomes queryable over time, not just a point-in-time email.
questions.professionalAnswer: With 40 databases, I'm not going to find regressions by waiting for someone to complain — that's reactive, and it means the client is finding problems before we are. So I lean on Query Store's history: it's already tracking every query's duration and resource usage over time, which means 'did this get slower' is a comparison query, not a live investigation. I'd write that comparison once — recent window versus a baseline window, flagged by a relative threshold weighted by how often the query actually runs — and then I wouldn't run it by hand against 40 databases either. I'd script it with PowerShell, loop it across every database on every server in the subscription, and schedule it as an Azure Automation runbook so it runs on its own, on a timer, without depending on anyone's laptop or memory. The output only matters to me as an exception report — if nothing regressed, I don't want an email at all, I want silence, and I want everything logged somewhere queryable so I can see regression trends over months, not just catch today's.
commonMistakes: Describes Query Store usage for a single database, not addressing how to scale across a fleet
Doesn't propose a relative/weighted threshold, flagging noise on rarely-run queries as equally urgent as hot-path regressions
Relies on someone manually running a script rather than automating it on a schedule (Azure Automation)
Doesn't log results centrally, losing the ability to see regression trends over time
keyPoints: Explains Query Store's persisted plan/runtime-stats history as the data source
Proposes a recent-vs-baseline window comparison with a relative, execution-count-weighted threshold
Automates the check across the whole fleet (PowerShell/dbatools looping over all databases)
Schedules it reliably via Azure Automation and centralizes results for trend visibility

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains how Query Store data enables regression detection
Proposes a sound comparison methodology (baseline, threshold, weighting)
Describes a realistic automation approach across many databases
Addresses reliable scheduling and centralized result tracking

questions.title: Managed Instance vs. Azure SQL Database vs. SQL Server on a VM: An Enterprise Decision Framework
questions.prompt: An enterprise client is migrating 80 databases from on-prem SQL Server, several of which use cross-database queries, linked servers, CLR assemblies, and SQL Agent jobs with complex dependencies. Walk through how you'd decide, database by database, which of the three Azure SQL deployment options each one belongs on.
questions.modelAnswer: I'd frame the decision around feature parity and management overhead, in that order, rather than defaulting to 'PaaS is always better.' Azure SQL Database is the right target for databases that are genuinely single-database in scope — no cross-database queries, no SQL Agent dependency the app can't live without, no linked servers, no unsupported CLR patterns — because it gets the most PaaS benefit: no OS or instance-level patching, built-in HA, and the broadest set of modern features (like Hyperscale) if needed. Azure SQL Managed Instance is the right target for the databases in this estate that need near-complete SQL Server surface-area compatibility but don't need full OS control: cross-database queries and transactions, SQL Agent jobs, Service Broker, linked servers, and CLR all work on Managed Instance in ways they simply don't on single Azure SQL Database, because Managed Instance presents an instance-level scope, not a single-database scope — this is exactly the profile described for several of the databases here. SQL Server on an Azure VM is the fallback for anything that needs something even Managed Instance doesn't fully support — specific OS-level dependencies, certain third-party tooling that assumes direct OS/filesystem access, FILESTREAM in configurations Managed Instance doesn't cover, or a version/feature combination not yet available on Managed Instance — accepting in exchange that the client now owns OS patching, SQL Server version upgrades, and backup infrastructure themselves, which is the most operational burden of the three options. In practice, for this specific estate, I'd triage database by database: anything using cross-database queries, linked servers, or Agent-job dependencies between multiple databases goes on Managed Instance by default, since splitting those dependencies apart to force them onto single databases is usually more migration risk than it's worth; databases using CLR get evaluated individually since Managed Instance supports CLR but with its own constraints worth verifying per assembly; and only the subset with no significant SQL Server surface-area dependency, is truly self-contained, goes to single Azure SQL Database, where it gets the most PaaS benefit. I would not assume the whole 80-database estate goes on one tier — that's usually a sign the assessment step was skipped.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd resist the instinct to pick one tier for the whole estate and instead run every database through the same filter: what does it actually depend on. Cross-database queries, linked servers, Agent job chains spanning multiple databases — those push a database toward Managed Instance immediately, because that's the one PaaS option that keeps near-full SQL Server compatibility at the instance level, and trying to re-architect those dependencies away just to force a database onto single Azure SQL DB is usually more risk than it's worth for a migration. CLR assemblies I'd check individually rather than assume either way — Managed Instance supports CLR, but I want to verify each assembly actually works under its constraints before committing. The databases that are genuinely self-contained, no instance-level dependencies at all, are the ones I'd push to single Azure SQL Database, because that's where you get the most hands-off PaaS benefit. SQL Server on a VM is my last resort, not a first choice — I'd only land there for something that needs OS-level access Managed Instance genuinely doesn't give you, and I'd make sure the client understands that choice means they're now the ones patching the OS and managing backups, not Azure.
commonMistakes: Picks a single deployment tier for the entire 80-database estate instead of assessing per-database dependencies
Doesn't recognize that cross-database queries, linked servers, and Agent jobs push toward Managed Instance specifically
Treats SQL Server on a VM as a default/easy choice instead of the highest-overhead fallback option
Assumes CLR support is binary (works/doesn't) rather than something to verify per assembly
keyPoints: Frames the decision around feature-parity needs, not a blanket preference
Correctly routes cross-database/linked-server/Agent-dependent databases to Managed Instance
Correctly reserves SQL Server on VM as the fallback with the most operational overhead
Proposes a realistic, per-database triage process rather than a single estate-wide decision

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the feature/compatibility differences across all three options
Correctly matches described dependencies (cross-db, linked servers, Agent) to Managed Instance
Proposes a sound per-database triage process for the estate
Acknowledges the operational tradeoff of SQL Server on a VM

questions.title: Elastic Pools: When Pooling Databases Helps and When It Backfires
questions.prompt: A SaaS client has 150 small, similarly-sized tenant databases, each individually provisioned and mostly idle except for short bursts of activity at different times of day. Someone proposes moving them all into a single elastic pool to save cost. Explain when that's the right call, and the scenario where pooling all 150 together would actually make things worse.
questions.modelAnswer: An elastic pool lets a group of databases share a single pool of compute (eDTUs or pooled vCores) and storage, billed once for the pool rather than per database, which is specifically valuable when individual databases have unpredictable, non-overlapping utilization spikes — exactly the profile described here, where 150 tenant databases burst at different times rather than all at once. The pool only needs enough capacity to cover the sum of concurrent peak usage across the pool at any given moment, not the sum of every tenant's individual peak, so if the bursts are genuinely staggered through the day, pooling can be dramatically cheaper than provisioning each database for its own worst case. The pooling decision becomes the wrong call under a specific, important condition: if the 150 tenants' burst patterns actually correlate — for example, if they all run a nightly batch job at midnight, or all see a traffic spike at the same regional business-hours peak — then the pool needs to be sized for the sum of simultaneous peaks anyway, at which point pooling adds the operational complexity of shared-resource contention (one noisy tenant degrading others sharing the pool) without actually delivering the cost benefit pooling is meant to provide, since you're provisioning for near-full simultaneous demand either way. In that correlated-peak scenario, keeping databases individually provisioned (or splitting them into multiple smaller pools grouped by actual, verified non-overlapping usage patterns) is the better design. Before recommending the pool, I'd pull actual DTU/vCore utilization history per database over at least a few weeks via Azure Monitor metrics to verify the bursts are genuinely staggered rather than assuming it from a general description, since 'different times of day' as stated by a stakeholder and 'different times of day' as shown by the metrics aren't always the same thing.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd say the pooling idea is right in principle, but I want to verify the assumption behind it before committing — pooling only saves money and works well when the tenants' usage bursts genuinely don't overlap, because the pool only has to be sized for the peak concurrent demand, not the sum of every tenant's individual peak. If they really are staggered through the day, this is exactly the right move and the savings can be substantial. But I've seen this backfire when it turns out everyone bursts at the same time — a nightly job, a regional business-hours spike — because then the pool needs almost the same total capacity as separate provisioning would have, except now you've also added shared-resource contention, where one noisy tenant can degrade the others. So before I recommend it, I'm pulling actual utilization metrics per database for a few weeks, not going off 'they burst at different times' as a verbal description, because that's exactly the kind of assumption that looks right until the bill or the complaints show up.
commonMistakes: Recommends pooling based on the stated scenario without verifying actual utilization overlap
Doesn't explain that pool sizing depends on concurrent, not individual, peak demand
Fails to identify correlated/simultaneous peak usage as the specific case where pooling backfires
Ignores the shared-resource-contention risk (noisy neighbor) introduced by pooling
keyPoints: Explains elastic pool cost mechanics (sized for concurrent peak, not sum of individual peaks)
Correctly identifies staggered, non-overlapping bursts as the scenario where pooling wins
Correctly identifies correlated/simultaneous peaks as the scenario where pooling backfires
Proposes verifying real utilization data before committing to the pooling decision

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains how elastic pool capacity/cost works
Correctly identifies the staggered-burst scenario as the good case for pooling
Correctly identifies the correlated-peak scenario as the failure case
Proposes verifying real usage data rather than assuming the stated pattern

questions.title: Zone-Redundant Configuration: What It Actually Protects Against
questions.prompt: A client assumes that enabling zone redundancy on their Azure SQL Database means they're protected against a regional Azure outage. Correct the misunderstanding, explain exactly what zone redundancy does protect against, and what they'd actually need for true regional protection.
questions.modelAnswer: Availability zones are physically separate datacenter groupings within a single Azure region, each with independent power, cooling, and networking, but still within that one region's geographic footprint and still dependent on that region's broader network backbone. Enabling zone redundancy on Azure SQL Database (available on Premium/Business Critical and certain Hyperscale configurations) places the database's replicas across multiple zones within the same region, so that if one zone experiences a localized failure — a power event or hardware failure affecting a specific datacenter cluster — the database fails over to a replica in a different zone within the same region, typically with no data loss and minimal downtime. That is real, valuable protection, but it is explicitly intra-region: it does nothing for a failure that affects the entire region, such as a region-wide network event, a major natural disaster affecting the whole metro area, or any Azure platform issue that isn't scoped to a single zone. True protection against a regional outage requires a cross-region strategy layered on top of zone redundancy, not instead of it: Active Geo-Replication or Auto-Failover Groups, which maintain an asynchronously replicated secondary database in a different Azure region entirely, with Auto-Failover Groups additionally providing the DNS-based listener endpoint that lets the application fail over without a connection-string change. I'd correct the client's assumption directly: zone redundancy protects against a datacenter-level failure within their current region, and they should absolutely keep it enabled, but it is not a substitute for geo-replication, and if 'we need to survive a regional outage' is a genuine business requirement with a defined RTO/RPO, they need both zone redundancy for intra-region resilience and a failover group for inter-region resilience, because these two features solve different scopes of failure and are not mutually exclusive — in fact a well-designed HA/DR architecture typically uses both together.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd correct this clearly and early, because it's a common and risky misunderstanding. Zone redundancy is real protection, but it's protection within one region — it spreads your replicas across physically separate datacenters that share the same region's network backbone, so it covers a datacenter-level failure, not a region-level one. If the whole region has a problem, zone redundancy doesn't help, because every zone it's using is still in that same region. For actual regional protection, they need a completely separate layer — a failover group replicating to a different Azure region entirely, which also gives them the DNS listener so the app doesn't need a connection-string change during failover. I'd be clear that this isn't an either-or — they should keep zone redundancy on for the datacenter-level protection it genuinely provides, and add a failover group on top of it if surviving a regional outage is a real requirement with a defined RTO and RPO, not just a nice-to-have.
commonMistakes: Conflates availability zones with separate Azure regions
Describes zone redundancy as sufficient for 'disaster recovery' without clarifying its intra-region scope
Doesn't mention Auto-Failover Groups' DNS listener benefit when proposing the cross-region fix
Presents zone redundancy and geo-replication as alternatives rather than complementary layers
keyPoints: Correctly explains availability zones as intra-region, physically separate datacenters
Correctly scopes zone redundancy's protection to datacenter/zone-level failures only
Proposes Auto-Failover Groups/geo-replication as the actual cross-region protection
Frames zone redundancy and cross-region replication as complementary, not either/or

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains what availability zones and zone redundancy actually protect against
Correctly identifies the gap (no regional protection) in the client's assumption
Proposes the correct cross-region mechanism (failover groups/geo-replication)
Frames both layers as complementary parts of a complete HA/DR design

questions.title: Azure SQL Auto-Failover Groups: The Listener Endpoint Is the Point
questions.prompt: A junior DBA sets up Active Geo-Replication to a secondary region and tells the team 'we have failover groups now.' Explain the actual difference between plain geo-replication and an Auto-Failover Group, and why that difference matters operationally during a real failover.
questions.modelAnswer: Active Geo-Replication and Auto-Failover Groups share the same underlying replication technology — an asynchronously replicated readable secondary in another region — but a failover group wraps that replication in two things geo-replication alone doesn't provide, and both matter enormously the moment an actual failover is needed. First, a failover group provides a read-write listener endpoint and a separate read-only listener endpoint, each a stable DNS name that transparently points at whichever database/region is currently primary — applications connect to the listener, not to a specific server name, so when a failover happens, the DNS record updates and the application reconnects to the new primary without any connection-string change, deployment, or manual intervention. With plain geo-replication, there's no such abstraction: failover means manually promoting the secondary and then someone has to update every application's connection string or configuration to point at the new server name, under pressure, during an incident — which is slow, error-prone, and exactly the kind of manual step that goes wrong during a real outage. Second, a failover group supports automatic failover policies with a configurable grace period, meaning Azure can detect an outage and fail over on its own within a defined RTO, rather than requiring a human to notice the outage, make the call, and execute the failover manually, which plain geo-replication requires every time. So 'we have failover groups now' said about a plain geo-replication setup is actually incorrect and operationally dangerous, because the team would discover during a real regional outage — the worst possible time — that they still need to manually re-point every application's connection string, with no automatic trigger, undermining whatever RTO they believe they've designed for. I'd correct this immediately and configure an actual failover group with the listener endpoints, specifically because the listener is the part that makes failover something applications survive without intervention rather than something that requires an emergency connection-string change across every environment.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd stop that statement right there, because it's not just imprecise, it's operationally dangerous if nobody catches it before an actual outage. Geo-replication and failover groups use the same replication underneath, but a failover group adds the one thing that actually matters during a real failover: a listener endpoint. That's a stable DNS name the app connects to instead of a specific server name, so when failover happens, DNS just points at the new primary and the app reconnects — no one has to touch a connection string. With plain geo-replication, there's no listener, so failing over means someone manually promotes the secondary and then someone else has to go update every app's connection string, under pressure, during the actual incident — that's a terrible time to be doing config changes by hand. Failover groups also support automatic failover with a grace period, so Azure can act without waiting for a human to notice and decide. I'd tell the team plainly: what you built is real replication, but it's not what 'we have failover groups' implies, and I want that fixed before we're relying on it during an actual regional outage, not during the postmortem after one.
commonMistakes: Treats geo-replication and failover groups as the same thing with different names
Doesn't identify the listener endpoint as the key operational difference
Misses that plain geo-replication requires manual connection-string updates across every application during failover
Doesn't mention automatic failover policy/grace period as an additional failover-group capability
keyPoints: Correctly explains both use the same underlying asynchronous replication
Identifies the read-write/read-only listener endpoints as the key differentiator
Explains the operational consequence: manual connection-string updates vs. transparent DNS failover
Mentions automatic failover policy as a second failover-group-specific capability

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains the shared replication technology underneath both
Correctly identifies the listener endpoint as the critical difference
Explains the real operational risk of lacking a listener during failover
Mentions automatic failover policy as an additional capability

questions.title: Microsoft Purview and Defender for SQL: Classification vs. Threat Detection
questions.prompt: A client's compliance team wants 'visibility into our sensitive data and protection against attacks' across 300 databases. Explain what Microsoft Purview's data discovery/classification and Microsoft Defender for SQL each actually do, why neither alone satisfies both halves of that request, and how they fit together.
questions.modelAnswer: These are two different products solving two different problems, and the compliance team's request actually has two distinct halves bundled into one sentence. Microsoft Purview (and Azure SQL's built-in Data Discovery & Classification, which feeds into Purview's broader catalog) scans schemas across databases, uses pattern matching and sensitivity-label rules to identify columns likely to contain sensitive data — SSNs, credit card numbers, health information — and lets the organization apply classification labels and maintain a searchable catalog of where sensitive data lives across the estate. That directly answers 'visibility into our sensitive data': it's a discovery and governance capability, answering the question 'what sensitive data do we have, and where.' It does nothing to detect or stop an attack in progress; it's a cataloging and labeling capability, not a monitoring one. Microsoft Defender for SQL is the other half: it provides vulnerability assessment (scanning for misconfigurations, missing patches, excessive permissions) and real-time threat detection (anomalous access patterns, potential SQL injection, brute-force login attempts, access from unusual locations), surfacing alerts when something looks like an actual attack or exploitable weakness. That answers 'protection against attacks' — it's a security monitoring and alerting capability, not a classification one. Neither alone satisfies the full request: Purview without Defender means the organization knows where its sensitive data is but has no active threat detection watching it; Defender without Purview means the organization has threat alerts but doesn't actually know which databases or columns hold the sensitive data those alerts are protecting, which matters for prioritizing response and for proving compliance scope. They fit together directly: Purview's classification results feed into how you prioritize and interpret Defender's alerts — an anomalous access alert against a database cataloged as containing SSNs and health data is a very different priority than the same alert against a database with no sensitive classifications, and Defender's vulnerability assessment findings often surface exactly the kind of misconfigured permission on a sensitive-classified table that Purview's discovery step flagged as worth protecting in the first place. At 300 databases, I'd roll out classification across the estate first (so the org actually knows its sensitive-data footprint), then make sure Defender for SQL is enabled everywhere and its alerts are triaged with that classification context in hand, rather than treating either as sufficient on its own.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd split their one request into the two separate things it actually is. 'Visibility into our sensitive data' is a cataloging problem — that's Purview and Data Discovery & Classification, scanning schemas and flagging columns that look like SSNs or health data, so you end up with an actual map of where sensitive data lives across 300 databases. 'Protection against attacks' is a monitoring problem — that's Defender for SQL, which does vulnerability scanning and real-time threat detection, flagging things like brute-force attempts or unusual access patterns. Neither one does the other's job — Purview won't warn you about an attack in progress, and Defender won't tell you which databases actually hold sensitive data. The reason I'd push for both together, not either alone, is that they make each other more useful — a Defender alert against a database Purview's already classified as holding SSNs is something I'd triage immediately, while the same alert against a database with no sensitive data is a lower priority. At 300 databases I'd get classification rolled out across the whole estate first, so by the time Defender starts generating alerts, the team already has the context to know which ones actually matter.
commonMistakes: Treats Purview/classification and Defender for SQL as interchangeable or redundant
Describes classification as providing threat detection, or Defender as providing data cataloging
Doesn't explain how classification context improves triage of Defender alerts
Recommends only one product as sufficient for the compliance team's full request
keyPoints: Correctly explains Purview/classification as a discovery and labeling capability
Correctly explains Defender for SQL as vulnerability assessment and threat detection
Identifies that the client's single request actually has two distinct halves
Explains how classification context improves alert triage, and vice versa

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly explains Purview/classification's capability and scope
Correctly explains Defender for SQL's capability and scope
Explains why neither alone satisfies the full compliance request
Proposes a sound combined rollout approach at estate scale

questions.title: PowerShell DSC and Azure Automation Runbooks for Fleet-Wide Configuration Drift
questions.prompt: Across 60 Azure SQL Managed Instances, you keep finding inconsistent database-scoped configuration settings (MAXDOP, cost threshold for parallelism) that drift because individual DBAs change them ad-hoc during troubleshooting and never revert. Explain how you'd use PowerShell automation to both detect and prevent this drift at fleet scale.
questions.modelAnswer: This is a configuration-drift problem, and it needs two separate automated capabilities: detection (finding drift that's already happened) and enforcement/prevention (stopping it from silently persisting). For detection, I'd write a PowerShell script using dbatools (Get-DbaSpConfigure or direct T-SQL against sys.database_scoped_configurations) that connects to every instance in the fleet — enumerated dynamically from Azure via Get-AzSqlInstance rather than a hardcoded list, so new instances are automatically included — pulls the current value of each setting I care about, and diffs it against a defined baseline/desired-state document (a simple JSON or PowerShell data file listing the expected value per setting). Any instance whose actual configuration doesn't match the baseline gets flagged in a report. For enforcement, rather than relying on that report being read and acted on manually, I'd schedule the same script (or a companion remediation script) as an Azure Automation runbook running on a timer, using a managed identity with the minimal permissions needed to both read and, where appropriate, automatically reset drifted settings back to baseline — though I'd be deliberate about which settings get auto-remediated versus just flagged for review, since some drift might reflect a legitimate, temporary troubleshooting change someone intended to make permanent and document, not a mistake. The cultural piece matters as much as the automation: I'd pair this with a lightweight change-request habit — if a DBA needs to change MAXDOP during an incident, the runbook's baseline file itself should be the place that change gets made and reviewed, ideally via a pull request against the config-as-code repo, rather than an ad-hoc ALTER DATABASE SCOPED CONFIGURATION run directly against the instance with nothing tracking it. That turns the baseline into the source of truth, and the runbook's job becomes keeping reality aligned with that tracked, reviewed baseline rather than the baseline just describing whatever's currently guessed to be deployed.
questions.professionalAnswer: I'd treat this as two problems, not one: finding drift that already happened, and stopping new drift from sticking around silently. For finding it, I'd write a PowerShell script with dbatools that walks every instance — pulled dynamically from Azure, not a list someone has to remember to update — checks the settings I care about against a baseline file, and reports anything that doesn't match. For stopping it, I wouldn't trust that report to get read and acted on by a human reliably, so I'd run that same check as a scheduled Azure Automation runbook, with a managed identity instead of stored credentials, and I'd decide carefully which settings it's safe to auto-remediate versus which ones just get flagged for a person to look at — because sometimes a DBA changed MAXDOP during an incident on purpose and just forgot to either revert it or document it as the new intended baseline. That's actually the real fix underneath the automation: the baseline needs to be the thing that changes first, ideally through a reviewed pull request, and the runbook's job is just keeping the fleet honest against whatever that baseline says — not the other way around, where the fleet's current state is treated as the truth and nobody can tell intentional change from drift.
commonMistakes: Proposes only a detection/reporting script without an enforcement or scheduling mechanism
Hardcodes the list of instances instead of enumerating them dynamically from Azure
Auto-remediates every setting without distinguishing intentional changes from accidental drift
Relies on a manually-run script instead of a scheduled Azure Automation runbook with managed identity
Doesn't treat the baseline/desired-state file as the actual source of truth requiring its own review process
keyPoints: Separates drift detection from drift enforcement/prevention as two distinct capabilities
Dynamically enumerates the fleet rather than hardcoding instance lists
Uses a scheduled Azure Automation runbook with managed identity, not manual or locally-run scripts
Distinguishes auto-remediable settings from ones needing human review
Frames the baseline/desired-state file as the reviewed source of truth, not the instances themselves

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correctly designs the drift-detection approach across a dynamic fleet
Proposes a sound scheduled enforcement mechanism (Azure Automation, managed identity)
Distinguishes auto-remediation from flagged-for-review changes thoughtfully
Connects the technical fix to a sustainable process (baseline as source of truth)

questions.title: PowerShell/dbatools Script to Audit Backup Health Across a Fleet
questions.prompt: Write a PowerShell script using dbatools that connects to every Azure SQL Managed Instance in a resource group, checks when each database's last full backup and last log backup occurred, and flags any database whose last full backup is older than 24 hours or whose last log backup is older than 30 minutes.
questions.code:
# Requires: Az module authenticated, dbatools installed
$resourceGroup = "rg-prod-sql"
$instances = Get-AzSqlInstance -ResourceGroupName $resourceGroup

$results = foreach ($instance in $instances) {
    $server = $instance.FullyQualifiedDomainName
    $dbs = Get-DbaDatabase -SqlInstance $server -ExcludeSystem

    foreach ($db in $dbs) {
        $lastFull = Get-DbaDbBackupHistory -SqlInstance $server -Database $db.Name -LastFull
        $lastLog  = Get-DbaDbBackupHistory -SqlInstance $server -Database $db.Name -LastLog

        [PSCustomObject]@{
            Instance       = $server
            Database       = $db.Name
            LastFullBackup = $lastFull.End
            LastLogBackup  = $lastLog.End
            FullBackupStale = ($null -eq $lastFull.End) -or
                               ((Get-Date) - $lastFull.End).TotalHours -gt 24
            LogBackupStale  = ($null -eq $lastLog.End) -or
                               ((Get-Date) - $lastLog.End).TotalMinutes -gt 30
        }
    }
}

$results | Where-Object { $_.FullBackupStale -or $_.LogBackupStale } |
    Format-Table Instance, Database, LastFullBackup, LastLogBackup -AutoSize
questions.modelAnswer: The script enumerates instances dynamically through Get-AzSqlInstance rather than a hardcoded list, so newly provisioned instances are automatically covered without anyone remembering to add them to a script. For each instance, Get-DbaDatabase pulls the real database list (excluding system databases, which have their own backup cadence and aren't the concern here), and dbatools' Get-DbaDbBackupHistory with -LastFull and -LastLog queries msdb's backup history directly rather than relying on anyone's assumption about when backups last ran. The staleness checks are deliberately written to treat a database with no backup history at all (LastFull.End is null) as stale too, not just old — a database that's never been backed up should fail this check loudly, not be silently skipped because the date comparison would otherwise throw or evaluate oddly against null. The thresholds (24 hours for full, 30 minutes for log) reflect typical Azure SQL default backup cadence, but I'd make them configurable parameters in a real version rather than hardcoded, since different databases may have different RPO requirements. The final filter only surfaces databases that are actually stale, so this is built to run unattended and produce an exception report, not a full inventory someone has to scan every time.
questions.professionalAnswer: I built this to answer one question only: which databases are at backup risk right now, across everything, without me having to check server by server. I pull the instance list straight from Azure so I'm never relying on a stale inventory list someone forgot to update. For each database, I'm not trusting 'it should have backed up' — I'm pulling the actual backup history from msdb through dbatools and checking real timestamps. The one detail I wouldn't skip is treating 'no backup history at all' as stale, not as a pass — if I don't explicitly handle that null case, a brand-new or broken database quietly slips through the filter instead of showing up as the most urgent thing on the list. And the whole point of the final filter is that I only want to see problems — if everything's healthy, I want an empty table, not a wall of green I have to scan through.

Doesn't handle the case where a database has no backup history at all (null comparison)
Hardcodes the staleness thresholds without acknowledging they should vary by RPO requirement
Returns the full inventory instead of filtering to only the stale/at-risk databases

Uses dbatools' actual backup-history cmdlets instead of assuming backup cadence
Correctly treats missing backup history as a stale/failing condition
Filters output to an exception report rather than a full dump

questions.title: Implementing Row-Level Security for a Multi-Region Sales Table
questions.prompt: Write the T-SQL to implement Row-Level Security on a Sales.Orders table so that users can only see rows matching their assigned region, stored in a UserRegionMap table, with a fallback that lets members of a 'GlobalReporting' database role see all rows regardless of region.
questions.code:
-- Mapping table: which region(s) each database user is allowed to see
CREATE TABLE dbo.UserRegionMap (
    DatabaseUserName SYSNAME NOT NULL,
    Region VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
    CONSTRAINT PK_UserRegionMap PRIMARY KEY (DatabaseUserName, Region)
);

-- Inline table-valued predicate function
CREATE FUNCTION Security.fn_RegionPredicate(@Region VARCHAR(50))
RETURNS TABLE
WITH SCHEMABINDING
AS
RETURN
    SELECT 1 AS fn_result
    WHERE IS_ROLEMEMBER('GlobalReporting') = 1
       OR EXISTS (
            SELECT 1
            FROM dbo.UserRegionMap urm
            WHERE urm.DatabaseUserName = USER_NAME()
              AND urm.Region = @Region
       );
GO

-- Security policy applying the predicate as a filter (SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE)
CREATE SECURITY POLICY Security.RegionFilterPolicy
ADD FILTER PREDICATE Security.fn_RegionPredicate(Region)
ON Sales.Orders
WITH (STATE = ON);
questions.modelAnswer: The predicate function is schema-bound and returns a single row (fn_result = 1) when access should be allowed, evaluated once per row of Sales.Orders against that row's Region value, which is exactly how RLS filter predicates work — they're not a one-time check, they're re-evaluated per row on every query. The IS_ROLEMEMBER('GlobalReporting') = 1 check is placed first and combined with OR, so a member of that role short-circuits straight to 'allowed' without needing a UserRegionMap entry at all, correctly implementing the described fallback. For everyone else, the EXISTS subquery checks whether the current session's USER_NAME() has an explicit mapping to that row's region in UserRegionMap — using USER_NAME() rather than a parameter passed by the application matters, because RLS's entire security value depends on the predicate being driven by the actual authenticated database principal, not by a value the client could potentially control or spoof in a connection parameter. The CREATE SECURITY POLICY statement applies this as a FILTER PREDICATE (rather than a BLOCK PREDICATE), which means rows failing the predicate are silently excluded from SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE results rather than raising an error — appropriate here since the goal is 'only see your region's rows', not 'reject any attempt to touch another region's data with an error'. I'd note that SCHEMABINDING on the function is required for it to be used in a security policy, and that this filter applies even to ad-hoc queries and ORM-generated SQL alike, which is the entire point of RLS over an application-layer WHERE clause that could be bypassed or simply forgotten in a new code path.
questions.professionalAnswer: I built the predicate so the global-access case is the first thing it checks — if you're in the GlobalReporting role, you're allowed, full stop, no need to even look at the mapping table. Everyone else gets checked against UserRegionMap using USER_NAME(), which is the actual authenticated database user, not anything the application passes in — that's the part that makes RLS actually trustworthy instead of just another filter the app could forget to apply. I applied it as a filter predicate rather than a block predicate on purpose, because the requirement here is 'just don't show them other regions,' not 'throw an error if someone tries' — those are different experiences and block predicates are for the second one. And the whole reason I'd reach for RLS instead of baking this into application code is that this predicate runs on every single query against the table, including anything ad-hoc someone writes in SSMS, so there's no code path where someone forgets to add the WHERE clause and leaks another region's data.
commonMistakes: Drives the predicate off a value passed from the application instead of USER_NAME()/session context
Forgets SCHEMABINDING on the predicate function, which is required for use in a security policy
Uses a block predicate when a filter predicate is what the requirement actually calls for
Doesn't account for the GlobalReporting fallback, or checks it in a way that still requires a region match
keyPoints: Correctly implements an inline table-valued schema-bound predicate function
Drives row visibility off USER_NAME()/session context, not an application-supplied value
Correctly implements the role-based fallback for GlobalReporting
Chooses filter predicate (not block) matching the stated requirement

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct, working predicate function and security policy syntax
Correctly drives access off USER_NAME()/session context
Correctly implements the GlobalReporting fallback
Chooses the right predicate type (filter vs block) with justification

questions.title: Bicep Template for a Compliant Azure SQL Database Deployment
questions.prompt: Write a Bicep template that deploys an Azure SQL Server and database with: Entra-only authentication, TDE enabled, a firewall rule allowing only Azure services, and tags identifying the environment and owner. Assume the Entra admin's object ID is passed as a parameter.
questions.modelAnswer: The key correctness detail here is that azureADOnlyAuthentication: true is set as part of the administrators block at server creation time, not as a separate step afterward — this provisions the server with SQL authentication already disabled from the start, which is both more secure (no window where SQL auth is briefly available) and avoids a second deployment or manual portal step to lock it down later. TDE is a child resource (transparentDataEncryption, name 'current') applied to the database with state 'Enabled' explicitly, even though TDE is on by default for new Azure SQL databases — I include it explicitly so the IaC is self-documenting and doesn't rely on an implicit platform default that could theoretically change. The firewall rule with startIpAddress and endIpAddress both set to 0.0.0.0 is the documented special-case convention Azure uses specifically to mean 'allow Azure services and resources to access this server' — it is not literally opening access to the IP 0.0.0.0, which is a common point of confusion; I'd call this out explicitly in a comment in real code since it looks alarming out of context. Tags are applied consistently on both the server and database resources, since tag-based cost allocation and ownership tracking typically needs to work at the database level, not just the server level. I deliberately did not add a broader public firewall rule or client IP rule, because the requirement was specifically 'only Azure services' — adding anything wider would silently violate the stated compliance requirement.
questions.professionalAnswer: The detail I'd point to first is that I set azureADOnlyAuthentication directly inside the administrators block at creation time, not as a follow-up step — that means this server is born with SQL auth already disabled, so there's no window where it's live and someone could create a SQL login before we lock it down. I added the TDE resource explicitly even though it's on by default, because I don't want this template's security posture depending on an assumption about a platform default — if someone reads this file, I want them to see TDE is on, not have to go check the portal to confirm it. The firewall rule is the one I'd flag in a code review comment, because 0.0.0.0 to 0.0.0.0 looks like it's opening the server to the whole internet, but it's actually Azure's specific convention for 'allow Azure services only' — I don't want a future reviewer to misread that and either panic or, worse, assume it's fine to widen it without understanding what it actually means.
commonMistakes: Sets azureADOnlyAuthentication as a separate post-deployment step instead of in the initial administrators block
Omits the explicit TDE resource, relying silently on the platform default
Misunderstands or misconfigures the 0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0 firewall rule as opening public access, or omits a comment explaining it
Forgets to apply tags consistently across both the server and database resources
keyPoints: Correctly sets Entra-only authentication at server creation via the administrators block
Explicitly enables TDE as a child resource rather than relying on an implicit default
Correctly implements the 'Allow Azure services' firewall rule convention
Applies tags consistently across server and database resources

evaluationCriteria.criterion: Correct Bicep resource structure and valid syntax
Correctly configures Entra-only authentication at creation
Correctly implements TDE and the Azure-services-only firewall rule
Correct, consistent tagging across resources
